SECTION: I. Ruddertowne (Pages 1-2)

TOPICS: legal appeal, conflict of interest, zoning ordinance, court decision, property development, federal lawsuit

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The case is C.A. No. 11A-06-001(ESB) before Judge E. Scott Bradley (Page 1)
- This is an unpublished opinion from the Superior Court of Delaware, dated August 30, 2012 (Page 1)
- The Westlaw citation is 2012 WL 3860732 (Del.Super.) (Page 1)
- Diane Hanson, a Dewey Beach town commissioner, voted in favor of an ordinance clarifying the height limit for structures in the RB-1 zoning district (Page 1)
- The Delaware State Public Integrity Commission (PIC) found Hanson violated the Code of Conduct due to conflicts of interest related to her rental properties and a pending lawsuit with Dewey Beach Enterprises (DBE) (Page 1)
- The Clarifying Ordinance stated the height limit was 35 feet and made retroactive to the 2007 Comprehensive Land Use Plan (Page 1)
- The court reversed the PIC's decision, finding it unsupported by substantial evidence and procedurally flawed (Page 1)
- DBE submitted a building permit and site plan for a three-story, mixed-use structure in early November 2007 (Page 2)
- The site plan would add a parking garage and 62 residential units to Ruddertowne (Page 2)
- Dewey Beach denied the application due to non-compliance with a 3,600 square-foot lot requirement per residential unit (Page 2)
- DBE appealed to the Board of Adjustment on January 23, 2008, and then to the Superior Court, which affirmed the denial (Page 2)
- The Delaware Supreme Court reversed the Superior Court's decision, finding the minimum lot requirement ambiguous (Page 2)
- On July 10, 2009, DBE and RRI filed a federal complaint against Dewey Beach and its officials (Mayor Tush, David King, Hanson, Hanewinckel) (Page 2)
- The complaint alleged violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, including substantive and procedural due process, equal protection, regulatory taking, civil conspiracy, and abuse of official power (Page 2)
- Dewey Beach filed a motion to dismiss the complaint, citing nine grounds for dismissal (Page 2)

SECTION: II. The Federal Case (Pages 2-3)

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- DBE submitted a building permit and site plan for a three-story, mixed-use structure in early November 2007 (Page 2)
- The site plan would add a parking garage and 62 residential units to Ruddertowne (Page 2)
- Dewey Beach cited a zoning code requiring a 3,600 square-foot lot for each residential unit as the reason for denial (Page 2)
- DBE appealed the denial to the Board of Adjustment on January 23, 2008, and then to the Superior Court, which affirmed the denial (Page 2)
- The Delaware Supreme Court reversed the Superior Court's decision, finding the minimum lot requirement ambiguous (Page 2)
- On July 10, 2009, DBE and RRI filed a federal complaint against Dewey Beach and its officials (Mayor Tush, David King, Hanson, Hanewinckel) (Page 2)

- The District Court granted Dewey Beach's motion to dismiss with respect to Count III (Equal Protection) and Counts VIII and IX (Equitable Estoppel), and denied its motion to dismiss in all other respects (Page 3)
- The 2007 Comprehensive Land Use Plan provided that "Relaxed bulk standards" were available for contiguous tracts of at least 80,000 square feet in the RB-1 zoning district (Page 3)
- The Clarifying Ordinance stated that "Relaxed bulk standards" do not permit any height increase beyond 35 feet, which is the maximum height in all zoning classifications in Dewey Beach (Page 3)
- The Clarifying Ordinance was adopted by a majority vote of the Commissioners on September 11, 2010, and applied retroactively to June 29, 2007 (Page 3)
- Joseph W. Nelson, a property owner, filed a five-page complaint against Hanson with PIC on October 1, 2010 (Page 3)

SECTION: VIII. Hanson's Arguments (Pages 6-15)

TOPICS: conflict of interest, jurisdiction, substantial evidence, qualified immunity, appearance of impropriety, competition between rental properties and hotel, legal standards, PIC findings

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The Clarifying Ordinance would limit DBE's structure to 35 feet, making it a less fearsome competitor to Hanson's rental properties (Page 6)
- Hanson had an impermissible conflict of interest due to her concern about quality of life from increased traffic and congestion (Page 6)
- Hanson was sued personally in a Federal Case, putting her at risk of paying a judgment and attorney's fees, and her attorney believed the ordinance would help her qualified immunity defense (Page 6)
- The standard of review is whether PIC's decision is supported by substantial evidence on the record (Page 6)
- Substantial evidence is defined as that which "a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion" (Page 6)
- Hanson argues PIC lacks jurisdiction because she is a town officer, not a State officer, and that the Code of Conduct does not apply to her (Page 6)
- The definition of "State employee" includes those receiving compensation from a State agency, appointed members earning over $5,000/year, and elected school board members (Page 7)
- The definition of "State agency" excludes political subdivisions like counties and municipalities (Page 7)
- Section 29 Del. C. § 5802(4) requires all counties, municipalities, and towns to adopt a code of conduct at least as stringent as the state's, or be subject to it by January 23, 1993 (Page 7)
- The Code of Conduct applies to Dewey Beach because it lacks an approved code of conduct (Page 7)
- Commissioner Hanson is an elected official of Dewey Beach, so PIC has jurisdiction over her (Page 7)
- Hanson argues that PIC's finding of a conflict of interest due to her two oceanside rental properties competing with a bayside hotel is not supported by substantial evidence (Page 7)
- PIC relied on a statement in Nelson's complaint that Hanson had previously said redevelopment would jeopardize her rental income, creating a conflict of interest (Page 7)
- Hanson's statement in a Cape Gazette interview dated September 12, 2007, is quoted (Page 8)
- Hanson stated that a 68-foot hotel/condo hybrid would "compete with property owners who rent their homes or for those selling their properties" (Page 8)
- The court found that Hanson did not state her own rentals would be competed with by DBE's hotel (Page 8)
- Hanson testified at the hearing that DBE's bayside hotel offered no competition for her ocean-side houses (Page 8)
- A tenant story about renting an oceanfront house for $1,500 more per week than a bay property was cited as evidence of the difference in value (Page 8)
- The court concluded that PIC's analysis of competition was overly simplistic and unsupported by substantial evidence (Page 8)
- PIC failed to examine or compare the price and nature of Hanson's rentals with DBE's hotel (Page 9)
- Hanson has two rental properties: Sea Mist Villa (three-story, four-bedroom, two-bath oceanfront house) and Sea Dune Villa (six-bedroom, four-and-one-half bath condominium) (Page 9)
- DBE proposed building a 120-room hotel on the bay in a commercial area (Page 9)
- The properties are separated by Coastal Highway, a busy four-lane highway (Page 9)
- There is no evidence about the prices charged by Hanson or planned for DBE (Page 9)
- PIC concluded Hanson voted for the Clarifying Ordinance to maintain her quality of life, but this finding violated its own rule requiring specific identification of alleged Code of Conduct violations (Page 9)
- PIC found Hanson had a conflict of interest because the Clarifying Ordinance could help her qualified immunity defense in the Federal Case (Page 10)
- The real purpose of the Clarifying Ordinance was, in part, to help Dewey Beach in the Federal Case, a purpose not disclosed to the public (Page 10)
- Hanson's lawyer told her the ordinance would help her qualified immunity defense (Page 10)
- PIC concluded Hanson was at risk for damages and attorney's fees simply because DBE sued her individually (Page 10)
- There is scant evidence in the record to support the finding that Hanson was at risk personally in the Federal Case (Page 10)
- The law does not require actual impairment of judgment, only that it may "tend" to be impaired (Page 10)
- The Clarifying Ordinance would set the height limit at 35 feet and make it retroactive, allowing Hanson to argue her past acts were official acts for which she is entitled to qualified immunity (Page 10)
- The Clarifying Ordinance had two purposes: clarifying bulk standards and helping Dewey Beach in the Federal Case (Page 11)
- Mandalas, Dewey Beach's attorney, publicly testified at a hearing that he recommended the ordinance for litigation purposes (Page 11)
- There is no evidence that Mandalas or Walton told Hanson the ordinance would help her personally in her defense (Page 11)
- The court notes that a conflict of interest only exists if Hanson voted to help her own defense, not the town's (Page 11)
- A direct quote from Mandalas: "I did, in fact, recommend that for litigation purposes, I thought this ordinance was an ordinance that should be adopted" (Page 11)
- A testimony excerpt shows Walton confirming they spoke about the potential impact of the ordinance on Hanson's qualified immunity defense (Page 11)
- PIC concluded Hanson "not only knew the purpose was not on the face, but was advised of the personal benefit to her if it passed" (Page 12)
- Walton testified he talked to Hanson about the Clarifying Ordinance's effect on her qualified immunity defense but never told PIC what his advice was (Page 12)
- There is no evidence in the record that Walton told Hanson the Clarifying Ordinance would help her qualified immunity defense (Page 12)
- Declaratory statutes are usually not given retroactive effect because they cannot reverse past court decisions or prejudice constitutional and vested rights (Page 12)
- The United States Supreme Court has ruled that the legislature cannot declare the construction of a previous act prejudicially affecting constitutional and vested rights (Page 12)
- DBE would have argued its right to build a 68-foot tall structure under the Relaxed bulk (Page 12)
- Qualified immunity balances holding public officials accountable with shielding them from harassment when acting reasonably (Page 13)
- A municipal employee has qualified immunity for governmental acts but is liable for ministerial acts (Page 13)
- The existence of qualified immunity turns on the objective reasonableness of actions, not the official's subjective intent (Page 13)
- To determine qualified immunity, a court must decide: (1) whether a constitutional right was violated, and (2) whether that right was clearly established (Page 13)
- The relevant inquiry is whether a reasonable officer would have known their conduct was unlawful (Page 13)
- The PIC never conducted this analysis because it never reviewed DBE's complaint against Hanson (Page 13)
- The PIC also never determined if Hanson's qualified immunity defense would overcome her conflicts of interest (Page 13)
- The court concludes there was not substantial evidence to support PIC's conflict of interest findings regarding Hanson's rental properties and qualified immunity defense (Page 14)
- The conflict of interest issue regarding Hanson's quality of life was not properly before PIC (Page 14)
- The appearance of impropriety test is based on whether conduct would create a perception that an official's ability to carry out duties with integrity, impartiality, and competence is impaired (Page 14)
- The mutual agreement and release had a two-step process: a vote in executive session to move it forward, followed by a public vote by the entire council to adopt it (Page 14)
- Mayor Hanson was the one nay vote on accepting or rejecting the proposed settlement (Page 14)
- The mutual agreement and release permitted a maximum height for DBE's structure of 45.67 feet (Page 14)
- The case is Hanson v. Delaware State Public Integrity Com'n, cited as 2012 WL 3860732 (Del.Super.) (Page 15)
- The court identifies two views of the evidence: Hanson voted to help her rental properties compete with DBE's hotel, or she voted because she opposed a project nearly twice as tall as other buildings in Dewey Beach (Page 15)
- The Delaware State Public Integrity Commission (PIC) chose the former view (Page 15)
- The court concludes the PIC's choice is not supported by substantial evidence in the record (Page 15)
- The decision of the Delaware State Public Integrity Commission is reversed (Page 15)
- The final order states "IT IS SO ORDERED." (Page 15)

SECTION: VIII. Hanson's Arguments (Pages 6-15)

TOPICS: conflict of interest, jurisdiction, substantial evidence, qualified immunity, appearance of impropriety, competition between rental properties and hotel, legal standards, PIC findings

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The Clarifying Ordinance would limit DBE's structure to 35 feet, making it a less fearsome competitor to Hanson's rental properties (Page 6)
- Hanson had an impermissible conflict of interest due to her concern about quality of life from increased traffic and congestion (Page 6)
- Hanson was sued personally in a Federal Case, putting her at risk of paying a judgment and attorney's fees, and her attorney believed the ordinance would help her qualified immunity defense (Page 6)
- The standard of review is whether PIC's decision is supported by substantial evidence on the record (Page 6)
- Substantial evidence is defined as that which "a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion" (Page 6)
- Hanson argues PIC lacks jurisdiction because she is a town officer, not a State officer, and that the Code of Conduct does not apply to her (Page 6)
- The definition of "State employee" includes those receiving compensation from a State agency, appointed members earning over $5,000/year, and elected school board members (Page 7)
- The definition of "State agency" excludes political subdivisions like counties and municipalities (Page 7)
- Section 29 Del. C. § 5802(4) requires all counties, municipalities, and towns to adopt a code of conduct at least as stringent as the state's, or be subject to it by January 23, 1993 (Page 7)
- The Code of Conduct applies to Dewey Beach because it lacks an approved code of conduct (Page 7)
- Commissioner Hanson is an elected official of Dewey Beach, so PIC has jurisdiction over her (Page 7)
- Hanson argues that PIC's finding of a conflict of interest due to her two oceanside rental properties competing with a bayside hotel is not supported by substantial evidence (Page 7)
- PIC relied on a statement in Nelson's complaint that Hanson had previously said redevelopment would jeopardize her rental income, creating a conflict of interest (Page 7)
- Hanson's statement in a Cape Gazette interview dated September 12, 2007, is quoted (Page 8)
- Hanson stated that a 68-foot hotel/condo hybrid would "compete with property owners who rent their homes or for those selling their properties" (Page 8)
- The court found that Hanson did not state her own rentals would be competed with by DBE's hotel (Page 8)
- Hanson testified at the hearing that DBE's bayside hotel offered no competition for her ocean-side houses (Page 8)
- A tenant story about renting an oceanfront house for $1,500 more per week than a bay property was cited as evidence of the difference in value (Page 8)
- The court concluded that PIC's analysis of competition was overly simplistic and unsupported by substantial evidence (Page 8)
- PIC failed to examine or compare the price and nature of Hanson's rentals with DBE's hotel (Page 9)
- Hanson has two rental properties: Sea Mist Villa (three-story, four-bedroom, two-bath oceanfront house) and Sea Dune Villa (six-bedroom, four-and-one-half bath condominium) (Page 9)
- DBE proposed building a 120-room hotel on the bay in a commercial area (Page 9)
- The properties are separated by Coastal Highway, a busy four-lane highway (Page 9)
- There is no evidence about the prices charged by Hanson or planned for DBE (Page 9)
- PIC concluded Hanson voted for the Clarifying Ordinance to maintain her quality of life, but this finding violated its own rule requiring specific identification of alleged Code of Conduct violations (Page 9)
- PIC found Hanson had a conflict of interest because the Clarifying Ordinance could help her qualified immunity defense in the Federal Case (Page 10)
- The real purpose of the Clarifying Ordinance was, in part, to help Dewey Beach in the Federal Case, a purpose not disclosed to the public (Page 10)
- Hanson's lawyer told her the ordinance would help her qualified immunity defense (Page 10)
- PIC concluded Hanson was at risk for damages and attorney's fees simply because DBE sued her individually (Page 10)
- There is scant evidence in the record to support the finding that Hanson was at risk personally in the Federal Case (Page 10)
- The law does not require actual impairment of judgment, only that it may "tend" to be impaired (Page 10)
- The Clarifying Ordinance would set the height limit at 35 feet and make it retroactive, allowing Hanson to argue her past acts were official acts for which she is entitled to qualified immunity (Page 10)
- The Clarifying Ordinance had two purposes: clarifying bulk standards and helping Dewey Beach in the Federal Case (Page 11)
- Mandalas, Dewey Beach's attorney, publicly testified at a hearing that he recommended the ordinance for litigation purposes (Page 11)
- There is no evidence that Mandalas or Walton told Hanson the ordinance would help her personally in her defense (Page 11)
- The court notes that a conflict of interest only exists if Hanson voted to help her own defense, not the town's (Page 11)
- A direct quote from Mandalas: "I did, in fact, recommend that for litigation purposes, I thought this ordinance was an ordinance that should be adopted" (Page 11)
- A testimony excerpt shows Walton confirming they spoke about the potential impact of the ordinance on Hanson's qualified immunity defense (Page 11)
- PIC concluded Hanson "not only knew the purpose was not on the face, but was advised of the personal benefit to her if it passed" (Page 12)
- Walton testified he talked to Hanson about the Clarifying Ordinance's effect on her qualified immunity defense but never told PIC what his advice was (Page 12)
- There is no evidence in the record that Walton told Hanson the Clarifying Ordinance would help her qualified immunity defense (Page 12)
- Declaratory statutes are usually not given retroactive effect because they cannot reverse past court decisions or prejudice constitutional and vested rights (Page 12)
- The United States Supreme Court has ruled that the legislature cannot declare the construction of a previous act prejudicially affecting constitutional and vested rights (Page 12)
- DBE would have argued its right to build a 68-foot tall structure under the Relaxed bulk (Page 12)
- Qualified immunity balances holding public officials accountable with shielding them from harassment when acting reasonably (Page 13)
- A municipal employee has qualified immunity for governmental acts but is liable for ministerial acts (Page 13)
- The existence of qualified immunity turns on the objective reasonableness of actions, not the official's subjective intent (Page 13)
- To determine qualified immunity, a court must decide: (1) whether a constitutional right was violated, and (2) whether that right was clearly established (Page 13)
- The relevant inquiry is whether a reasonable officer would have known their conduct was unlawful (Page 13)
- The PIC never conducted this analysis because it never reviewed DBE's complaint against Hanson (Page 13)
- The PIC also never determined if Hanson's qualified immunity defense would overcome her conflicts of interest (Page 13)
- The court concludes there was not substantial evidence to support PIC's conflict of interest findings regarding Hanson's rental properties and qualified immunity defense (Page 14)
- The conflict of interest issue regarding Hanson's quality of life was not properly before PIC (Page 14)
- The appearance of impropriety test is based on whether conduct would create a perception that an official's ability to carry out duties with integrity, impartiality, and competence is impaired (Page 14)
- The mutual agreement and release had a two-step process: a vote in executive session to move it forward, followed by a public vote by the entire council to adopt it (Page 14)
- Mayor Hanson was the one nay vote on accepting or rejecting the proposed settlement (Page 14)
- The mutual agreement and release permitted a maximum height for DBE's structure of 45.67 feet (Page 14)
- The case is Hanson v. Delaware State Public Integrity Com'n, cited as 2012 WL 3860732 (Del.Super.) (Page 15)
- The court identifies two views of the evidence: Hanson voted to help her rental properties compete with DBE's hotel, or she voted because she opposed a project nearly twice as tall as other buildings in Dewey Beach (Page 15)
- The Delaware State Public Integrity Commission (PIC) chose the former view (Page 15)
- The court concludes the PIC's choice is not supported by substantial evidence in the record (Page 15)
- The decision of the Delaware State Public Integrity Commission is reversed (Page 15)
- The final order states "IT IS SO ORDERED." (Page 15)

Hanson: A 120-unit 5-star condo/hotel complex is not a town center. I would like to see a third option of a mixed-use complex that follows our current zoning laws at a height of 35 feet—one that is truly a town center.
